implementation_notes: The classic private-constructor structure survives in C#, but thread-safe lazy creation is library business: a static readonly Lazy<T> (System.Lazy<T>, .NET 4.0+) with the default LazyThreadSafetyMode.ExecutionAndPublication replaces double-checked locking and caches a failed initialisation's exception. When early creation is acceptable, a plain static readonly field initialiser replaces it as well, because the runtime runs static field initialisers inside the type-initialisation lock and calls the static constructor at most once. Note the documented order: a static field initialiser that creates the instance runs before the static constructor body.
pitfalls: A Lazy<T> built from a factory caches the exception: every later access rethrows the same failure, so retry logic must live inside the factory.
Static field initialisers run before the static constructor, so setup code placed in the static constructor executes after the instance already exists - the classic C# singleton ordering surprise.
Blocking inside a static initialiser (locking, waiting on another type's initialiser, a blocking .Result) can deadlock the type-initialisation lock.
Deserialisation or reflection (Activator.CreateInstance, serializers that bypass constructors) can produce a second instance; guard the constructor where that matters.

variants.name: Static readonly field with type-initialisation lock
variants.idiom_name: static readonly field initialiser (+ optional static constructor)
variants.implementation_notes: The oldest and shortest C# form: a static readonly field initialised inline, with the CLR's type-initialisation lock making the initialisation run at most once and publishing it to all threads, so neither Lazy<T> nor explicit locking is needed. The trade is timing - the runtime may initialise the type early (beforefieldinit) rather than exactly at first access - and error shape: a throwing initialiser surfaces as TypeInitializationException and is cached for the lifetime of the AppDomain.
pitfalls: The initialisation point is not guaranteed to be the first access (beforefieldinit permits early initialisation), so do not hang expensive startup work off it.
A failing initialiser throws TypeInitializationException on every later access instead of retrying.
Adding a static constructor suppresses beforefieldinit and changes the timing: do it deliberately.
